## Visual Identity

LocalFirst uses **one four-color system** across the website and future brand materials. It is warm, grounded, tactile, and high-contrast—the visual equivalent of showing up in person and doing the work with your own hands.

### Core palette

| Role | Hex | Name | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Foundation | `#2C2C2C` | Graphite | Full-bleed backgrounds, primary dark text, navigation, and footer |
| Primary action | `#EE7828` | Bright Brick | Buttons, active states, links, review stars, and decisive emphasis |
| Calm neutral | `#C5BAAA` | Concrete | Editorial sections, secondary copy on Graphite, dividers, and quiet balance |
| Supporting surface | `#806D61` | Craft | Raised panels, warm depth, transition glows, and secondary moments |

White may be used as a utility text color where contrast requires it; it is not a fifth brand accent. Any lighter or darker supporting tone must be derived from the four core colors rather than introducing blue, gold, green, or another decorative hue.

### Contrast pairings

- **Graphite on Bright Brick** for action buttons and highlighted panels.
- **Concrete on Graphite** for supporting copy and interface labels.
- **White on Craft** for longer text on raised warm surfaces.
- **Graphite on Concrete** for editorial reading sections.

**Heading font:** Instrument Serif

**Body / UI font:** Inter

**Vibe:** An editorial Colorado field journal with cinematic polish. Graphite supplies authority, Concrete and Craft make it feel human and physical, and Bright Brick creates the decisive moment that moves an owner to act.

### Imagery style
Owner-shot documentary. Real Colorado storefronts, real owners, real food, shot on-site with professional gear. **No stock. No AI-generated filler.** This is not a taste preference — it is the product, and the site says so in those words.

> **Color rule:** Bright Brick owns action and emphasis. Concrete creates breathing room. Craft adds tactile depth. Graphite carries the brand. Do not scatter all four colors into every component; let each section have one dominant field and one clear accent.

## Origin & Story

Nicholas Molina founded LocalFirst after watching good local businesses close — "not because they were bad at what they do, but because they were invisible online." He had built websites for restaurants in Albuquerque back in the early 2000s, and came back to the work with a harder constraint: he would only serve businesses he could physically drive to.

He is a **Google Local Guide, Level 7** — Google's own platform verifying him as a Top 1% contributor — and **BBB A+ accredited**. He operates solo. He knocks on the doors himself, shoots the photos himself, and answers the Ask Maps questions himself, on camera, standing in the business.

The line that ends the story on the site is the line that ends everything: **"That's not going to happen on my watch."**

---

## Mission

To make sure the customers who are already looking for a local Colorado business can actually see why they should choose it — by putting real, current, human-made proof on the profile that decides the sale.

## Vision

A Front Range where no brick-and-mortar business loses a customer to a stale photo, an unanswered review, or an AI guessing on their behalf. **No Business Left Behind.**

---

## Core Values

1. **Show, don't claim.** Every assertion is either a public number the reader can check themselves or a photo taken on their sidewalk. The site literally teaches the reader how to audit their own profile before it sells them anything.
2. **Physical presence.** "All three happen on your sidewalk." What can't be faked and can't be outsourced is the whole business model.
3. **Ground truth over guesswork.** When a profile goes unanswered, AI invents an answer. LocalFirst exists to put the real answer where the machine will read it. *"Ground-truth in. Guesswork out."*
4. **Attack the neglect, never the owner.** Seven out of ten businesses set the profile up once and never touch it again. The owner isn't lazy — they're running a business. The profile is the failure, not the person.
5. **Honest fit.** "No pressure. If it's not a fit, I'll tell you." The walk-away is a feature.

---

## Brand Archetype

**Primary: The Caregiver.** The mission is protective — the enemy is a business dying quietly, and Nicholas positions himself as the one standing between the owner and that outcome. Warmth, obligation, "on my watch," "no business left behind."

**Secondary: The Everyman-Expert (Sage inflection).** He is a guy with a camera and a truck who happens to hold a credential Google itself issued. The expertise is delivered in plain, checkable language — never from a podium. The Sage shows up as *teaching owners how to audit what customers see*, never as *lecturing*.

The blend is what makes it work: a pure Sage would be a consultant, a pure Caregiver would be a charity. LocalFirst is a neighbor who knows exactly how the machine works and will show you for free before charging you anything.

## Tone & Voice

**Voice adjectives: Direct. Grounded. Protective.**

### The five signature moves

These are the mechanics that make the copy sound like Nicholas. Use at least two per page.

**1. The verify-it-yourself instruction.**
Instead of claiming a problem exists, hand the reader the steps to find it themselves.
> "Pull up your Google Business Profile. Two minutes on your phone. Every number is public."

**2. The fragment stack.**
Three to four short declaratives, no conjunctions, building rhythm into a landing.
> "DIY. Every week. No exceptions."
> "No stock. No filler."
> "Ground-truth in. Guesswork out."
> "Someone hears about you. They look you up. Then they decide."

**3. Number in place of adjective.**
Never "extensive experience." Always the figure.
> "Level 7." "Top 1% contributor." "Within 48 hours." "2–5 fresh photos." "About 7 out of 10." "15 recent visits." "5.0 across 19 Google reviews."

**4. The absolution.**
Name the gap, then immediately remove the shame from it.
> "If those numbers surprised you, you're not alone. About 7 out of 10 local businesses set up their profile once and never touch it again."

**5. The honest close.**
End on a low-pressure, high-trust note that costs the sale sometimes.
> "No pressure. If it's not a fit, I'll tell you."

### DO

- Write **"I," never "we."** One person does this work; the copy has to say so. "Here's how I actually do this." "I'll come to you." "Let me handle all of it for you."
- Address the owner as **"you," and their business as "your business."** The reader is always the subject of their own sentence.
- **Lead with the customer's experience, not the technology.** "The profile customers see before they visit." The GBP is a first impression, not a listing.
- **Use present tense and active voice.** "Customers are already looking." "AI decides."
- **State the geography as a boundary you chose.** "Colorado only." "Denver / Aurora metro." "Brick-and-mortar businesses only." Constraints read as credibility here, never as apology.

### DON'T

- **Don't use adjectives where a number exists.** "Amazing results" is a banned phrase; "5.0 across 19 Google reviews" is the same claim, checkable.
- **Don't blame the owner.** No "you've been neglecting," no "your profile is a mess," no shame framing. The neglect is the villain; the owner is the person you're protecting.
- **Don't write agency-speak.** No "leverage," "solutions," "synergy," "digital transformation," "cutting-edge," "holistic," "we're passionate about." The testimonials on the site use this language — that's the customer's voice, not the brand's. Never mirror it back.
- **Don't hedge or over-qualify.** No "we can help you potentially improve." Say the thing: "Video is the strongest single local ranking signal AI uses. Full stop."
- **Don't manufacture urgency with fake scarcity.** Real deadlines only — "before the 2026 holiday season" works because it's an actual season. "Limited spots!" does not.
- **Don't say "SEO" as the headline promise.** The site sells a *first impression that converts attention already present*. SEO is a mechanism, not the pitch.

### Sentence rhythm

Long setup, short landing. Set the scene in one full sentence, then drop a fragment on it.

> "Google's new AI search surfaces customer questions on your profile — about your hours, your menu, your service, your parking. When those questions go unanswered, AI fills the gap with guesses. I show up in person and answer them on video. **Ground-truth in. Guesswork out.**"

Em dashes for the aside. Periods where a comma would be softer. Never a semicolon.

## Brand Vocabulary

### Own these words

| Term | Why it's ours |
|---|---|
| **No Business Left Behind** | The mission line. Ends pages; never opens them. |
| **On my watch** | The founder's personal stake, in four words. |
| **First impression** | The reframe: a GBP is not a listing, it's the doorway. |
| **On-site / in-person / on your sidewalk** | The differentiator that can't be outsourced. |
| **Ground truth** | What Nicholas puts in; the opposite of what AI guesses. |
| **Google Local Guide · Level 7** | Always written with the level. Never just "Local Guide." |
| **Top 1% contributor** | Google's language, not ours — that's why it lands. |
| **Ask Maps answers** | The 2026-specific service almost nobody else offers. |
| **Two minutes on your phone** | The frictionless audit invitation. |
| **Every number is public** | Permission to verify; the trust unlock. |
| **Real businesses. Real visits.** | Portfolio framing, print and web. |
| **No stock. No filler.** | The production standard, stated as a refusal. |
| **Brick-and-mortar** | Who this is for, said plainly. |
| **Denver / Aurora metro · Front Range** | Never "the Colorado area." Name the streets. |
| **Local businesses. Stronger communities. A brighter Colorado.** | The civic ladder — use as a closer, sparingly. |

### Avoid these words

`leverage` · `solutions` · `synergy` · `cutting-edge` · `world-class` · `passionate` · `robust` · `seamless` · `game-changer` · `we're excited to` · `industry-leading` · `holistic` · `unlock your potential` · `digital transformation`

Also avoid **"we"** in any sentence describing the work. It is factually wrong and it erases the entire differentiator.

## Customer Transformation

**Before:** A confident owner with a genuinely good business and a quiet, sinking suspicion that the phone should be ringing more than it does. They know the profile exists. They set it up years ago. They avoid looking at it, because looking at it means confronting something they don't have time to fix — and no one has told them what fixing it would even involve.

**After:** They pull up their own profile and it looks like the business they actually run. The photos are from this season. The reviews have replies. The questions have answers, in their own voice, on video. The nervous feeling is gone, and it's been replaced with something closer to pride — they'd show it to someone on purpose now.

> **Copy implication:** the emotional payload is *relief and pride*, not *growth and ROI*. Write to the owner who wants to stop being embarrassed by their own listing, and the revenue argument lands on its own.

---

## The Enemy

**Invisibility that nobody chose.**

It has three faces, and web copy should name whichever one fits the page:

1. **The stale profile** — a great business represented by a four-year-old photo, an unanswered review, and hours that changed last spring.
2. **The guessing machine** — 2026's escalation. AI no longer just lists businesses; it decides whether to recommend them, reading whatever the profile says. Unanswered means invented.
3. **The remote agency** — services that never visit, use stock photography, generate filler, and can't produce a Level 7 signal. Named by contrast, never by company: *"No agency in Colorado works this way."*

The enemy is never the business owner. Ever.

---

## Competitive Positioning

**The local field:** Denver/Aurora GBP work is split between national white-label SEO shops that never set foot in the state, freelance marketers managing profiles remotely from a laptop, web agencies where GBP is a checkbox on a bigger retainer, and Google's own free tools that assume the owner has time.

**What LocalFirst can claim that they cannot:**

- A **Google-issued Level 7 Local Guide account** posting to the profile — a trust signal an agency can't buy or assign.
- **On-site capture on every single deliverable.** Photos, video, 360° tours, Ask Maps answers, all shot in the building.
- **A named human with a face and a direct cell number**, in a category built on anonymous account managers.
- **Geographic refusal.** Colorado only, brick-and-mortar only, on-site only — narrow enough that the promise is provably keepable.

**The white space:** *AI-era ground truth, captured in person.* Everyone else is either selling "local SEO" (a mechanism nobody buys emotionally) or selling remote profile management (which cannot answer an Ask Maps question about the parking lot). The unclaimed position is being **the person who physically goes to the business and tells the machine the truth about it** — before the machine makes something up. That position is currently empty in Colorado, and the site is one of very few places in the market already speaking in 2026 terms.

---

## Unique Value Proposition

**LocalFirst is the only Colorado service where a Google-verified Level 7 Local Guide personally drives to your business, shoots the photos and video himself, and answers the AI's questions on-site — so the profile that decides your next customer shows the business you actually run.**

---

## Brand Promise

We promise every customer that everything on their profile came from a real visit to their real business — no stock, no filler, no guesses — and that if LocalFirst isn't the right fit, they'll hear that first, for free, before anyone talks about price.

## Website Content Angles

Five recurring angles for site pages, blog posts, and landing pages. Each one is drawn from the transformation, vocabulary, or enemy above — they are not generic content buckets.

**Angle 1 — The Two-Minute Audit.** Hand the reader an exact, checkable procedure for finding a gap in their own profile. Ends with the absolution, never a scold.
> *Example hook:* "Open Google Maps. Search your own business. Tap Photos, then By Owner. Look at the date."

**Angle 2 — What The Machine Sees.** Explain, in plain language, what AI actually reads on a profile and what it does when the answer isn't there. The 2026 differentiator; nobody local is writing this.
> *Example hook:* "When a customer asks Google whether you have parking and your profile says nothing, AI doesn't stay quiet. It guesses."

**Angle 3 — On The Sidewalk.** Document a real visit. Business name, neighborhood, what was shot, what changed. Proof of the thing that can't be outsourced.
> *Example hook:* "Tuesday morning, Sheesh Salon, Denver. Forty minutes, one camera, and a profile that finally looks like the room."

**Angle 4 — The Credential Nobody Can Buy.** Explain what Level 7 means, why Google issued it, and why a source signal is different from a service.
> *Example hook:* "Google decides who it trusts. It already decided about my account — here's what that's worth on your profile."

**Angle 5 — Great Businesses Deserve To Be Seen.** The mission angle. Why a good business goes quiet, why that's not the owner's fault, and what "No Business Left Behind" actually commits to.
> *Example hook:* "Somewhere in Aurora tonight, a family is eating worse food at a chain — because the better place had worse photos. That's the whole problem in one sentence."

## Voice Test

Before publishing any page, check all six. Four or fewer means rewrite.

- [ ] Is there at least one **number the reader could verify themselves**?
- [ ] Does it say **"I"** and never "we"?
- [ ] Is there a **fragment stack** landing at least one section?
- [ ] Does it **name the neglect without blaming the owner**?
- [ ] Would it **still be true if the reader checked**?
- [ ] Does the close **give the reader an honest out**?
